lesson.title: Your Dictionary's Built-In Toolkit
lesson.summary: A dictionary is not just a container you index into with square brackets. It carries a set of built-in methods for reading, changing, and combining its data safely.
lesson.body:
You already know that a dictionary stores key value pairs and that you can read a value with square brackets, like prices["apple"]. That works fine as long as the key is guaranteed to exist. The moment you are not sure, square brackets become risky: asking for a missing key does not return None or an empty result, it crashes your program with a KeyError. Dictionary methods exist to give you safer, more flexible ways to work with a dict, so you are not stuck relying on square brackets for everything.

A method is simply a function that belongs to an object and is called with dot notation, object.method(). Because a dictionary is an object, it comes with its own family of methods you can call on any dict you create. The ones you will use constantly are get, keys, values, items, update, and pop, and you will meet each of them in its own chapter. For now, the important idea is that these methods split into two groups: some let you look at a dictionary's contents without changing it (get, keys, values, items), and others let you change the dictionary itself (update, pop, and a few more like clear and setdefault).

Here is a quick look at a few of them working together on the same dictionary.

inventory = {"apples": 10, "bananas": 5, "cherries": 20}
print(len(inventory))
print(inventory.get("bananas"))
print(list(inventory.keys()))

This prints 3, then 5, then ['apples', 'bananas', 'cherries']. len() is a built-in function that works on a dict because a dict knows how to report its own size, get("bananas") safely looks up the value stored under "bananas", and keys() returns all the keys, which we wrap in list() so it prints as a familiar list. Since Python 3.7, dictionaries remember the order you inserted items in, which is why the keys come back in the same order they were added: apples, then bananas, then cherries.

Learning these methods is what turns a dictionary from 'a thing I can index into' into 'a thing I can query, update, and safely explore.' Every chapter that follows in this unit is really just zooming in on one member of this toolkit.
